title: Tiny AI Pets Turn Everyday Objects Into Needy Friends
summary: Your plant is thirsty, but you forgot to water it again. A tiny screen on the pot shows a sad little plant pet, drooping sadly. Suddenly, watering it feels very important. That is the idea behind OATs, short for Object Agent Twins: tiny AI pets on small E Ink screens that pair with everyday things. Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student at Carnegie Mellon University, made them. She showed the project at a computing meeting in Detroit in early November and won two Honorable Mention awards. The idea comes from Tamagotchi, egg-shaped toys from the 1990s that held digital pets you had to care for, and Kim wanted to bring that caring feeling to real objects. Each OAT has a small screen joined to sensors that check moisture, temperature, humidity, light and motion. The main part costs about $20. The faces come from Google's Gemini image tool and change as the sensors change. Put one on a skateboard, and if it sits still for days, the pet looks sad. Ride it, and it cheers up. The demo also started a debate: some people worry cute, emotional robots could make us trust AI too much. Kim says that is why OATs keep things small.
why_it_matters: It could help you remember to water your plants, ride your skateboard, and take care of the things you own.

background_read: OATs are tiny digital pets that live on small screens attached to everyday objects like plant pots and skateboards.
Sensors check things like water, light, and movement, and the pet's face changes to show how the object is doing, which reminds people to take care of it.
The idea comes from Tamagotchi, small toy pets from the 1990s that owners had to feed and look after.
